fields.title: The Key Teachings of G. K. Chesterton
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of G. K. Chesterton’s Christian teaching — wonder and gratitude, the madness of reason cut loose, the paradoxes and the romance of orthodoxy, joy as the Christian secret, tradition and the common man, the uniqueness of man, the strangest story in the world, and the faith that keeps rising from its grave — weighed honestly where evangelical readers part company with him. Fifteen short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as an independent companion. Orthodoxy and The Everlasting Man are in the Ochorus library.
fields.about_html:
This is a companion to G. K. Chesterton, not a book by him. Written by Ochorus, it sets out in fifteen short chapters the teaching for which Chesterton is chiefly remembered — the wonder and gratitude he learned in the nursery, the madman who has lost everything except his reason, the thought that stops thought, the cosmic loyalty that loves the world enough to change it, the furious opposites that Christianity holds together, orthodoxy as the great adventure, joy as the gigantic secret of the Christian, tradition as the democracy of the dead, humility in its right place, the dignity of ordinary life, the man in the cave and the God in the cave, the strangest story in the world, the five deaths of the faith, and the holy gaiety of St Francis. It adds a chapter on his life, a conclusion, and a guide to his books.

It is important to be clear about what this book is and is not. It is an independent work of exposition, summary and appreciation, not published by, affiliated with, or endorsed by any society or body devoted to Chesterton’s memory or his cause. Two of his greatest books, Orthodoxy (1908) and The Everlasting Man (1925), are in the public domain and in the Ochorus library, and short sentences from them are quoted sparingly here, each checked against the library’s own text and named by book and chapter. Nothing is quoted from his later works that are still in copyright; those are described in our own words. Scripture is quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version.

Chesterton wrote Orthodoxy as a member of the Church of England and was received into the Roman Catholic Church in 1922. This volume says plainly where evangelical readers will differ from his later convictions — on the authority of the Church, on Mary and the saints, on the sacraments — and where his politics and economics are opinion rather than doctrine. It also faces honestly the antisemitic passages in some of his writing, which a fair modern companion must name. He would have wanted the argument, and he would have wanted readers to go past him to Christ.

The best way to use this book is beside his own. Orthodoxy and The Everlasting Man are both in the Ochorus library; read them alongside these chapters.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. 1 CORINTHIANS 3:19

There are Christian writers who are admired, and there are Christian writers who are enjoyed. G. K. Chesterton is one of the very few who is both. He was a London journalist who wrote too much and too fast, a huge, untidy, absent-minded man in a cloak and a wide-brimmed hat, who once, the story goes, telegraphed his wife from a railway station to ask where he was supposed to be. He never studied theology and would have laughed at being called a theologian. Yet in an age that was quite sure it had outgrown the Christian faith, he defended it so cheerfully, so cleverly and so generously that even his opponents loved him, and more than a century later readers are still finding in his books that the old faith is larger, stranger and gladder than they had been told.

He did not come to faith by a straight road. As a young art student in the 1890s he passed through a season of near-despair, in which the fashionable pessimism of the day almost swallowed him. He came out of it holding on, as he later said, by a thin thread of gratitude: the overwhelming sense that it was good to exist at all. Slowly, and largely by thinking for himself, he found that the instincts he had learned in the nursery — wonder, thanks, loyalty, the sense that joy hangs on keeping some small condition — fitted the Christian creed like a key in a lock. He told that story in Orthodoxy, the book that has done more than any other of his to bring doubters to Christ, and he spent the rest of his life telling it again in other forms.

Why he still matters

Chesterton matters, first, because he restored wonder to the faith. Many Christians defend their beliefs as though they were a burden to be carried, a set of hard sayings to be accepted with a sigh. Chesterton defended them as though they were good news, which they are. He saw the world as a gift that need not have been given, every dandelion and lamp-post a small astonishment, and he argued that only the Christian account of things explains why the world feels like that, and why we feel that we ought to say thank you for it.

O give thanks unto the Lord; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever. PSALM 136:1

He matters, second, because he saw where unbelief leads. He lived at the high tide of confidence in reason, science and progress, and he noticed, long before most, that a reason cut loose from God does not end in freedom but in madness, and that a culture which doubts everything will soon doubt its own power to think. Much that he predicted has come to pass. His warnings read today less like the opinions of an Edwardian journalist than like a description of our own century.

He matters, third, because he was a joyful fighter. He loved an argument and chose the biggest opponents he could find, and he never once lost his temper or his friendships in the course of it. He debated George Bernard Shaw for thirty years and remained his friend. He crossed swords with H. G. Wells and was still welcome at his house. In an age of anger, he is a model of how a Christian can contend earnestly for the faith without contempt for those who reject it.

How this book is arranged

After a chapter on his life, fifteen short chapters set out his teaching. The first group follows the road of Orthodoxy itself: the wonder and gratitude he called the ethics of elfland; the madman who has lost everything except his reason; the thought that stops thought; and the cosmic loyalty that loves the world enough to change it. The second group turns to what he found when he came to the creed: the furious opposites that Christianity holds in balance; orthodoxy as the most thrilling of adventures; joy as the Christian’s gigantic secret; tradition as the democracy of the dead; humility in its proper place; and the dignity of ordinary life. The third group follows The Everlasting Man: the man in the cave, who is unlike any other creature; the God in the cave at Bethlehem; the strangest story in the world, which is the story of Christ; and the five deaths of the faith, from each of which it has risen. A last teaching chapter turns to St Francis of Assisi, in whom Chesterton saw the holy joy he loved best. A conclusion follows, and a guide to his books.

Each chapter ends with points for reflection and a prayer. Chesterton said grace before everything — before meals, before books, before the theatre, before dipping his pen in the ink — and a book about him that did not end each chapter in thanks would miss the point. Read slowly, a chapter at a time, with a Bible open.

A word about his words

Chesterton died in 1936. Orthodoxy (1908) and The Everlasting Man (1925) are in the public domain, and both are in the Ochorus library. This companion quotes from them sparingly — a single sentence here and there, each checked against the library’s own text and named by book and chapter — because no summary can quite catch the sound of him, and because the quotations are meant to send the reader to the books themselves. Some of his later books, among them St Thomas Aquinas (1933) and his Autobiography (1936), remain in copyright in some countries, and nothing of them is quoted here; they are described in our own words. Readers should also be warned that a great many sayings attributed to Chesterton on the internet are not his at all. Nothing in these pages is quoted from memory or from a collection of sayings.

Where he must be read with care

This is not a book of hero-worship. Chesterton is a delight and a guide, but there are places where evangelical readers will part company with him, and one place where every reader must be honest about him. It is kinder to name them at the start.

First, his church. Orthodoxy was written when Chesterton was a member of the Church of England, and it defends the faith of the Apostles’ Creed rather than the claims of any one church; that is why Christians of every tradition have loved it. But in 1922 he was received into the Roman Catholic Church, and his later books defend its distinctive claims with the same energy. He came to believe that the Church of Rome is the one true teacher of the faith, carrying an authority that evangelicals believe belongs to Scripture alone. He prayed to Mary and the saints and wrote poems in honour of the Virgin. He held the Catholic understanding of the sacraments, and he said that the chief reason he became a Catholic was to have his sins absolved by a priest. Evangelical readers will differ from him on all of these points, and the chapters that touch on them weigh them briefly and, we hope, charitably.

Second, his politics. Chesterton, with his friend Hilaire Belloc, championed an economic programme called distributism, which held that property should be spread as widely as possible, so that as many families as possible owned their own land, shop or workshop. There is much wisdom in his love of the small and the local, and much of his criticism of both big business and big government has worn well. But distributism is an economic opinion, not a Christian doctrine, and Christians who love Chesterton have held every kind of view about it. The same is true of many of his opinions on the questions of his day, from the Boer War to Irish home rule. Chapter twelve considers this.

Third, and most painful: some of what Chesterton wrote about Jews was wrong, and it has rightly been called antisemitic. During the Marconi affair of 1912 and 1913, a scandal in which government ministers were found to have traded in shares connected with a government contract, Chesterton, his brother Cecil and Belloc attacked those involved in language that made much of their being Jewish. In his journalism, and in some of his verse and fiction, Jews appear as stock figures of money and rootlessness. In The New Jerusalem (1920), an account of a journey to Palestine, he argued that the Jews were a separate nation dwelling among other nations, and proposed — insisting that he meant it seriously — that Jews holding high office in England should wear a distinctive dress so that everyone might know they were foreigners. These things are not the inventions of his critics. They are on the page, and no appeal to the habits of his time makes them right. It is also true, and fairness requires that it be said, that he condemned the Nazi persecution of the Jews early and without reserve: in 1933, when many in Britain were still inclined to excuse the new German government, he told a Jewish newspaper that he was appalled by Hitler’s atrocities, and that he and Belloc would be found defending the last Jew in Europe. Scholars still disagree about how deep the prejudice ran. When, in 2019, the Roman Catholic bishop of the diocese in which Chesterton lived and died declined to open a cause for his canonisation, he named it as one of his reasons.

This companion does not excuse those passages, and it does not draw on them. The faith Chesterton defended was first preached by Jews, about a Jewish Messiah, from Jewish Scriptures, and a Christian who speaks with contempt of the people from whom Christ came according to the flesh has forgotten something essential about his own religion. The right response is the one Scripture gives to every believer who has spoken carelessly of his neighbour: to call it sin, to learn from it, and not to repeat it.

To whom pertaineth the adoption, and the glory, and the covenants, and the giving of the law, and the service of God, and the promises; whose are the fathers, and of whom as concerning the flesh Christ came, who is over all, God blessed for ever. Amen. ROMANS 9:4–5
Out of the same mouth proceedeth blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not so to be. JAMES 3:10

None of these points is raised to diminish him. They are raised because a fair companion owes them to its readers, and because Chesterton himself loved nothing better than a man who said plainly what he thought. He hated hero-worship and would have been the first to say that he was a sinner, as he was the first to say that he was a fool.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21

Where Chesterton is faithful — and on the great matters of the creed, the incarnation, the cross and the resurrection, he is faithful and glorious — receive it gladly. Where he goes beyond what is written, mark it and test it by Scripture. He would not have wanted you to follow him. He would have wanted you to follow Christ, and to enjoy the world He made.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. When did you last feel simple wonder at the fact that the world exists? Write down one ordinary thing you have stopped noticing, and thank God for it today.

2. Think of someone you know who regards Christianity as dull, or as a set of rules. Pray for that person by name as you read this book.

3. Decide how you will read: one chapter a day or a week, with a Bible open and a few minutes of thanksgiving after each prayer.

4. Open Orthodoxy in the Ochorus library and read its short preface and first chapter alongside this introduction.

5. Ask God to give you a mind that thinks clearly, a heart that is grateful, and a tongue that speaks of others with charity.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You made the world out of nothing, and You did not have to make it at all.
Thank You for the servants You have given Your church, who have made the old faith shine again for those who thought it dull.
As I read about one of them, keep me from admiring him and forgetting You, and keep me honest about his faults as I would want others to be honest about mine.
Give me eyes to see Your gifts, a heart to thank You for them, and a love for every neighbour that has no room for contempt, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

fields.title: From Kensington to Beaconsfield
fields.body_html:
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. JAMES 1:17

A toy theatre. Gilbert Keith Chesterton was born on the twenty-ninth of May, 1874, in Kensington, in west London, the elder son of Edward Chesterton, whose family ran a firm of estate agents, and Marie Louise Grosjean, whose family was of Swiss and French descent. His brother Cecil, five years younger, became his lifelong companion and sparring partner; the two boys argued, it was said, from the day Cecil could talk, and never stopped. Their father was a gentle, inventive man with a gift for hobbies, and he built his sons a toy theatre, with painted scenery and cardboard characters and a tiny proscenium arch. Gilbert never forgot it. The first thing he could remember, he used to say, was a young man with a golden crown crossing a little cardboard bridge, and all his life he saw the world rather like that: a bright, small, astonishing stage on which something tremendous was being played.

The home was kindly, liberal and only loosely religious. The boys were taken to hear a Unitarian minister, but Christianity in any definite form hardly touched them. Gilbert grew up on fairy tales, ballads, pictures and the great English writers, and on long arguments at the family table.

A dreamy schoolboy. At St Paul’s School in London he seemed to his teachers slow and absent-minded, a tall, shambling boy who drew in the margins of his books. But with a circle of friends he founded a debating club and a little magazine, and found that he could write. In 1893 he enrolled at the Slade School of Art, part of University College London, to train as an illustrator, and attended lectures in English literature on the side.

The dark years. Those years at the Slade became the darkest of his life. The artistic world of the 1890s was full of a weary, clever pessimism, a sense that nothing was real and nothing mattered, and the lonely young student breathed it in. He fell into what he afterwards described as a kind of madness. He filled notebooks with morbid and disturbing drawings. He and Cecil played with the planchette and the Ouija board, and he came away convinced of two things: that something was moving the board, and that whatever it was, it told lies. He gave it up, sickened, feeling that he had been meddling with something evil. He came close, he later believed, to losing his reason, or his soul.

Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O Lord. Lord, hear my voice. PSALM 130:1–2

A thread of thanks. What brought him back was not, at first, an argument. It was gratitude. Even at the lowest point, he said, he had clung to one thin thread: the sheer conviction that existence is good, that it is better to be than not to be, that a dandelion is a gift and not a matter of course. From that thread he began, slowly and largely by his own thinking, to rebuild a view of the world. In the notebooks of those recovering years he wrote that other people said grace before meals, but he would say grace before plays and concerts, before opening a book, before sketching, swimming, fencing, walking and dancing, and before he dipped his pen in the ink. It was the habit of the rest of his life.

Frances. In 1896 he met Frances Blogg, the eldest daughter of a family in Bedford Park, an artistic suburb of west London full of people who talked about religions. What astonished him about Frances was that she actually practised one. She had been brought up an Anglo-Catholic; she went to church, she prayed, and she seemed entirely untouched by the fashionable moods around her. He fell in love with her almost at once. They were married on the twenty-eighth of June, 1901, at St Mary Abbots, Kensington. Through her faith, and the clergy and Anglican friends she brought into his life, Chesterton found his way into the Church of England. It was a deeply happy marriage, though one marked by the sorrow of having no children. Their house was nonetheless always full of other people’s children, for whom he drew pictures and staged plays in his own toy theatre.

Whoso findeth a wife findeth a good thing, and obtaineth favour of the Lord. PROVERBS 18:22

Fleet Street. Chesterton left the Slade without a degree and went to work for a publisher, but he soon found his true calling in journalism. He wrote reviews and essays for The Speaker and the Daily News, and from 1905 he wrote a weekly column for the Illustrated London News, which he kept up for the rest of his life. He became one of the best-known figures in Fleet Street, the street of newspapers: a huge man, well over six feet and broad in proportion, in a cloak and a wide-brimmed hat, carrying a swordstick, his pince-nez never quite straight. He was famously absent-minded. He was also extraordinarily productive. In his lifetime he published some eighty books, hundreds of poems, about two hundred short stories and several thousand essays.

The great debates. He loved an argument, and he picked the biggest opponents he could find. In 1903 and 1904 he answered the atheist editor Robert Blatchford in the pages of The Clarion. For thirty years he debated George Bernard Shaw, in print and on public platforms, and the two men remained affectionate friends throughout. He argued with H. G. Wells about socialism, progress and history. In all of these quarrels he held that the instincts of ordinary people — for home, for property, for freedom, for faith — were wiser than the theories of the intellectuals who despised them.

Heretics and Orthodoxy. In 1905 he published Heretics, a book of essays on the leading thinkers of his day, from Kipling to Shaw, arguing that each of them had got something important wrong. Its critics, among them the writer G. S. Street, complained that he had attacked everybody else’s philosophy without ever stating his own. Chesterton accepted the challenge. His answer, published in 1908, was Orthodoxy. It was not a textbook of theology but, in his own phrase, “a sort of slovenly autobiography”: an account of how he personally had come to believe. He tells it as the story of a man who set out to discover a new truth and found, to his embarrassment, that it had all been discovered already.

Thus saith the Lord, Stand ye in the ways, and see, and ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein, and ye shall find rest for your souls. JEREMIAH 6:16

In the same year he published The Man Who Was Thursday, a wild nightmare of a novel about anarchists and detectives that turns, at the end, into something like a vision of the day of judgement. He had already written The Napoleon of Notting Hill (1904), and in 1911 he published The Ballad of the White Horse, a long poem about King Alfred and the Christian hope against overwhelming odds, which was quoted to the nation in the darkest days of the Second World War.

Father Brown. On a lecture tour in Yorkshire in 1904 he met a young Roman Catholic priest, Father John O’Connor, who became one of his closest friends. Chesterton was astonished to discover that this shy, gentle man knew more about the evil in the human heart than any worldly undergraduate. From that surprise came Father Brown, the small, round, unremarkable priest who solves crimes because, having heard so many confessions, he understands sin from the inside. The first collection, The Innocence of Father Brown, appeared in 1911, and the stories have been read and filmed ever since.

Beaconsfield. fields.title: The Ethics of Elfland
fields.body_html:
When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; what is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him? PSALM 8:3–4

The most famous chapter of Orthodoxy begins in the nursery. Chesterton said that his first and last philosophy, the one he believed in with unbroken certainty, he had learned not from philosophers but from fairy tales — from the nurse who told them and the common people who had handed them down. He did not mean that fairy tales are true in the sense that a history book is true. He meant that they had taught him the right attitude to the world, long before he had any religion, and that this attitude turned out, years later, to fit the Christian faith exactly.

The world is magic

The first thing fairy tales teach, Chesterton said, is that the world is not a machine. In the stories, apples are golden and trees bear jewels and a frog may be a prince, and the child accepts all of it without surprise. Grown-up people, by contrast, think that they have explained a thing when they have noticed that it happens regularly. They talk of the laws of nature as if the fact that leaves are green and the sun rises in the east were somehow necessary, as necessary as the fact that two and two make four. But it is not. There is no reason in logic why grass should be green rather than scarlet, or why an egg should become a bird rather than a fish. These things are not necessities. They are wonders that happen to be repeated, and the right response to a wonder is not an explanation but astonishment.

He went further. We tend to assume that repetition is a sign of something dead and mechanical, like a clock. But children, who are full of life, love repetition. They want the same story, the same game, the same joke, over and over again. It may be, Chesterton suggested, that God is like that — not too tired to vary the world, but strong enough to delight in doing the same glorious thing for ever. In the chapter called The Ethics of Elfland he put it in one of his best-known sentences: “It is possible that God says every morning, ‘Do it again’ to the sun; and every evening, ‘Do it again’ to the moon.” And a little later: “It may be that He has the eternal appetite of infancy; for we have sinned and grown old, and our Father is younger than we.”

While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night shall not cease. GENESIS 8:22
They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness. LAMENTATIONS 3:23

Gratitude

The second thing fairy tales teach is gratitude. The world is not owed to us. It is a gift, and a surprising one, and a gift implies a giver. Long before he believed in God, Chesterton felt that he ought to thank someone for the fact that he existed at all, and for dandelions and sunsets and the shape of his own hands. He put it in the same chapter with great simplicity: “The test of all happiness is gratitude; and I felt grateful, though I hardly knew to whom.” Children, he went on, are grateful to Santa Claus for the toys in their stockings; might he not be grateful to someone for putting two miraculous legs in his own?

This is one of the deepest things he ever wrote, and it is profoundly biblical. The Scriptures everywhere treat thanksgiving not as a pleasant addition to religion but as close to its heart, and the failure to give thanks as close to the heart of sin. When Paul describes the human race turning away from God, the first thing he says of it is not that it became wicked but that it became ungrateful.

Because that, when they knew God, they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish heart was darkened. ROMANS 1:21

The doctrine of conditional joy

The third thing fairy tales teach is what Chesterton, with mock solemnity, called the doctrine of conditional joy. In every fairy tale the happiness of the hero hangs on a single condition, often an apparently arbitrary one. Cinderella may go to the ball, but she must be home by midnight. The princess may live in the palace, but she must not open a certain door. The lovers may be happy, but one of them must not look back, or speak a certain word, or eat a certain fruit. The whole wonderful world of the story depends upon one small prohibition.

The modern mind finds this irritating. It asks why the condition should be kept, since no reason is given. But the child does not ask that, and Chesterton thought the child was right. If someone gives you a palace and asks only that you leave one door shut, it is a strange ingratitude to complain about the door. The joy is enormous; the condition is small; and the joy is a gift that could not have been demanded. He saw at once what this had to do with ordinary morality. To complain that marriage requires faithfulness, or that pleasure requires restraint, is like complaining that Cinderella has to leave the ball at midnight. It is to forget that the ball was a gift in the first place.

And the Lord God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat: but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it. GENESIS 2:16–17

It is not hard to see where this leads. The first story in the Bible is a story of conditional joy. A garden is given, every tree in it but one; and the whole tragedy of the human race begins with the refusal to keep a single small condition.

The world as a shipwreck

The last thing Chesterton drew from the nursery was a sense that the good things of the world are precious because they are rescued. He compared himself to Robinson Crusoe, who counts every object he has saved from the wreck — a knife, a barrel of powder, a few tools — with a kind of awe, because each is all he has and each might have been lost. That, he said, is how the good things of the world ought to look to us: not as a dull inventory, but as treasures saved from a ship that went down. Every ordinary thing is a survivor.

When he came at last to Christianity, he found that it told him exactly this. The world is good, because God made it. The world is also fallen, so that its goodness is not to be taken for granted. And the whole of it is held in being moment by moment by a Giver to whom thanks are owed.

The earth is the Lord’s, and the fulness thereof; the world, and they that dwell therein. PSALM 24:1

Weighing it

There is almost nothing in this chapter to set aside, and a great deal to receive with joy. Chesterton’s sense of wonder and his insistence on gratitude are a sorely needed tonic for believers who have come to treat the faith as a list of duties. Two cautions may be added.

The first is that wonder is not yet faith. A man may feel the strangeness and the gift of the world all his life and never turn to the Giver; and the Scriptures are clear that the witness of creation, though real, leaves us without excuse rather than with salvation. Chesterton knew this. His gratitude led him to look for the One to thank, and he found Him in the creed. The reader should not stop where Chesterton started.

The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork. PSALM 19:1

The second is that Chesterton’s happy account of the conditions of joy can make obedience sound easier than it is. The fairy tale’s one small condition becomes, in the Christian life, a daily cross; and the reason we keep God’s commands is not finally that they are small, but that He is good. Chesterton would have agreed. But the reader who has found a command of God anything but small should know that he is not the first, and should look not to the fairy tale but to the Saviour who kept every command in his place.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Look out of the window, or at your own hand, and try to see it as Chesterton did — as something that need not have existed at all. What do you notice?

2. Read Romans 1:18–23 and notice the place of thanklessness in Paul’s account of human sin.

3. Is there a command of God that you have resented as an arbitrary condition on your happiness? Bring it to Him with thanks for the gifts that surround it.

4. Make a list, as Crusoe did, of the things you have been given that you could not survive without. Thank God for each.

5. Read the chapter of Orthodoxy called The Ethics of Elfland, in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You made the sun and You call it up each morning, and You have never grown tired of Your world.
Forgive me for growing old in the wrong way, for taking Your gifts for granted, and for forgetting to say thank you.
Give me the eyes of a child who sees that everything is given, and the heart of a child who knows that the Giver is good.
Where You have set a condition on my joy, help me to keep it gladly, for the sake of Jesus Christ, who kept every one of Your commands for me. Amen.

fields.body_html:
Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools. ROMANS 1:22

Chesterton begins the argument of Orthodoxy proper in an unexpected place: the lunatic asylum. He had a reason. The modern world, he said, had given up believing in sin, but it had not yet given up believing in madness. Everyone could still agree that there is such a thing as a mind that has gone wrong. If he could show what madness really is, he could show something about the sane mind, and about the faith that keeps the mind sane.

The man who has lost everything except his reason

The common view is that a madman is a man who has lost his reason. Chesterton argued that the opposite is nearer the truth. In the chapter called The Maniac he wrote: “The madman is not the man who has lost his reason. The madman is the man who has lost everything except his reason.”

He explained what he meant. A man who believes himself to be the victim of a vast conspiracy is not, in the ordinary sense, illogical. If you argue with him, he has an answer for everything. Every piece of evidence you offer can be fitted into his theory: if people are kind to him, it is because they are trying to deceive him; if they are not, it proves his point. His explanation is complete, and it is perfectly consistent. What is wrong with it is not that it is irrational, but that it is small. It is a perfect circle, and a very narrow one. He has shut himself into a tiny world, and he cannot get out, because his reason, working with terrible efficiency, keeps closing every door.

What the madman has lost is everything that a healthy mind brings alongside its reason: humour, charity, common sense, the willingness to be surprised, the ordinary certainties of experience that a man knows even when he cannot prove them. It is these, not logic, that keep a man sane.

Be not wise in thine own eyes: fear the Lord, and depart from evil. PROVERBS 3:7

The modern madnesses

Chesterton then turned the picture on the philosophies of his day. The materialist, who holds that everything in the universe, including the human mind, is the product of blind physical causes, has exactly the madman’s kind of explanation. It is complete; it accounts for everything; and it leaves out everything that matters most, including the very freedom and reason by which the materialist claims to have discovered it. The man who holds that nothing is real except his own mind is in the same case. Each has a perfect circle of thought, and each is imprisoned in it.

The cure, Chesterton argued, is not more reasoning but more room. A sane man has always lived with mystery. He has kept one foot in the world of plain fact and the other in a world he cannot fully explain, and he has been content to let some things stay unexplained. In the same chapter Chesterton put it in four words: “Mysticism keeps men sane.” By mysticism he did not mean visions or trances. He meant the ordinary humility of a mind that knows it is not the measure of all things.

The circle and the cross

At the end of The Maniac he offered a picture that sums up the whole book. The symbol of the madman’s reason is the circle: perfect, complete, closed in upon itself, and unable to grow. The symbol of the Christian faith is the cross. At its centre there is a collision, two beams meeting at right angles, a contradiction that reason cannot smooth away — God and man, justice and mercy, death and life. But because it has a paradox at its heart, it can stretch out its arms for ever without changing its shape. “The cross opens its arms to the four winds,” he wrote; “it is a signpost for free travellers.”

For the preaching of the cross is to them that perish foolishness; but unto us which are saved it is the power of God. 1 CORINTHIANS 1:18

The only doctrine that can be proved

In the same chapter Chesterton made one of his most quoted remarks about sin. The modern theologians of his day, he observed, were inclined to deny original sin — the doctrine that human nature itself is corrupted and inclined to evil. He thought this absurd, because original sin is the one Christian doctrine that anyone can check for himself. “Certain new theologians dispute original sin,” he wrote, “which is the only part of Christian theology which can really be proved.” A man has only to read a newspaper, or look honestly into his own heart, to see the evidence.

The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? JEREMIAH 17:9
For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God. ROMANS 3:23

Weighing it

Chesterton’s diagnosis of a reason cut loose from humility is one of the most penetrating things in modern Christian writing, and it is deeply scriptural. Paul says that the wisdom of the world, turned against God, ends in folly; Chesterton showed how, in particular cases, it happens.

A caution belongs here. Chesterton was a defender of reason, not its enemy, and he said so plainly in the next chapter. But a careless reader can take from him the notion that thinking is dangerous and feeling is safe, or that faith means not asking questions. That is not what he meant, and it is not what Scripture teaches. The Bible calls us to love God with all our mind, and the cure for a bad argument is a better one. What Chesterton opposed was not reason but reason that refuses to bow — reason that has made itself God.

And thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength. MARK 12:30

A second caution concerns the word mysticism, which in Chesterton means something healthy and modest. The reader should not confuse it with the mystical techniques and private revelations that some have sought in place of Scripture. Chesterton’s mysticism was the humility of a man who knows that God is greater than his thoughts; and that humility is best learned by sitting under the Word that God has spoken.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Think of a time when you were completely convinced you were right and turned out to be wrong. What had you left out of the picture?

2. Are there areas of your life where you have built a closed circle of explanation — about a person, a grievance, or God Himself — that no evidence can break? Ask God to open it.

3. Read 1 Corinthians 1:18–31 slowly. Notice how Paul sets the cross against the wisdom of the world.

4. Look honestly at your own heart this week. Where do you see the evidence for original sin?

5. Read the chapter of Orthodoxy called The Maniac, in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Lord, You made my mind, and You did not make it to be its own god.
Forgive me for the times I have shut myself into small circles of my own reasoning, and refused to be surprised by You.
Keep me sane with the sanity of humility. Let me think hard and kneel low.
And keep before my eyes the cross of Jesus Christ, which opens its arms to all the world, and on which my sin was borne. Amen.

fields.title: The Thought That Stops Thought
fields.body_html:
And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free. JOHN 8:32

The second argument of Orthodoxy follows directly from the first. Chesterton had shown that madness lies in reason cut off from everything else. Now he set out to show that the modern world was in danger of something worse: of losing faith in reason itself. He called the chapter The Suicide of Thought, and it reads today like a prophecy.

Reason needs defending

He began by making clear that he was on reason’s side. The chapter on the madman, he said, had not been meant to attack the authority of reason; the whole aim was to defend it, because it needed defending. The great danger of his age was not too much reasoning but a growing doubt whether reasoning could reach the truth at all.

The point is simple and devastating. Every argument, every science, every inquiry, assumes that our minds can grasp something real. But that assumption cannot itself be proved by argument, because every argument depends on it. “It is idle to talk always of the alternative of reason and faith,” Chesterton wrote in this chapter. “Reason is itself a matter of faith.” If our thoughts are only the by-products of chemistry, there is no reason to trust them, including the thought that they are only chemistry. The sceptic who doubts everything must, sooner or later, doubt his own doubting.

The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. PSALM 14:1

The thought that stops thought

From this Chesterton drew his conclusion. There is one kind of thought that ought to be stopped, and it is the thought that stops all thought: the idea that the mind cannot know anything, that truth is only a matter of taste, that every belief is as good as every other because none of them can be true. “There is a thought that stops thought,” he wrote. “That is the only thought that ought to be stopped.” He believed that the authority of the Christian religion had always stood, among other things, as a defence of the human mind against that idea. The church had insisted that there is truth to be known, and in doing so it had kept the door open for thinking itself.

He then surveyed the fashionable creeds of his day — the worship of the will, the cult of the superman, the restless revolt against every standard — and showed how each of them, pressed to its conclusion, ended in the same place: a world in which it is impossible to say that anything is better than anything else. The man who rebels against everything, he said, has lost the right to rebel against anything; for to rebel is to appeal to a standard, and he has abolished all standards.

Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness. ISAIAH 5:20

Humility in the wrong place

In the middle of the chapter comes a passage that has been quoted ever since, about humility. In the old days, Chesterton said, humility was meant to restrain a man’s pride and ambition, while leaving him confident about the truth. The modern world had reversed this. Modern people were bold about themselves — their rights, their desires, their opinions of their own worth — and timid only about truth, which they hardly dared to say they knew. “A man was meant to be doubtful about himself, but undoubting about the truth,” he wrote; “this has been exactly reversed.” The result, he warned, would be a generation too modest to believe in the multiplication table.

It is hard to read that sentence today without a shiver of recognition. We live among people who are certain of their own goodness and uncertain whether anything is true. Chesterton saw that this is not humility at all, but a peculiar kind of pride: the refusal to be bound by anything outside oneself.

Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches: but let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me. JEREMIAH 9:23–24

Truth as a gift

Christianity, as Chesterton came to see it, does not ask a man to give up his mind. It gives his mind back to him. It says that the world is real, that God made it rational, that the human mind is made in His image and fitted to know it, and that truth exists and can be found. That is why, historically, the Christian faith has been the cradle of so much learning. A man who believes that God has spoken, and that God is truth, has every reason to think hard.

In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. JOHN 1:1

Weighing it

This chapter is among the most prophetic things Chesterton wrote, and evangelical readers will find little in it to set aside. Its insistence that truth is real and knowable, and that the mind is a gift of God to be used, stands squarely on Scripture.

Two points may be added. First, Chesterton’s confidence in the human mind needs to be balanced by Scripture’s realism about it. The mind is God’s gift, but it is also fallen, and it is often bent by the will to believe what it wants. Reason alone did not bring Chesterton to faith, and it will not bring anyone else; the Spirit of God must open the eyes.

But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God: for they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned. 1 CORINTHIANS 2:14

Second, when Chesterton speaks of religious authority as the guardian of the mind, the reader should remember where, for Christians of the Reformation, that authority finally rests. Chesterton came in time to locate it in the teaching office of the Roman Church. Evangelicals locate it in the written Word of God, by which every church and every teacher must be judged. The truth that sets us free is the truth spoken by Christ and written by His apostles.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Have you absorbed, perhaps without noticing, the idea that religious truth is only a matter of personal taste? How would your faith change if you really believed it was true?

2. Where are you bold about yourself and timid about the truth? Where should it be the other way round?

3. Read John 8:31–36 and notice how Jesus connects truth, freedom and Himself.

4. Choose one question about the faith that you have been afraid to think about, and study what Scripture says about it this week.

5. Read the chapter of Orthodoxy called The Suicide of Thought, in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Lord, You are the truth, and You have made my mind to know You.
Forgive me for being proud about myself and timid about You, for doubting what You have said and trusting what I feel.
Guard me from every thought that would stop thought, and open my eyes by Your Spirit to see what is real.
Make me humble about myself and unashamed of Your truth, and keep me in the freedom that Jesus Christ has given. Amen.

fields.title: The Flag of the World
fields.body_html:
For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life. JOHN 3:16

Once he had cleared the ground, Chesterton turned to a question that had troubled him since the dark years at the Slade: what is the right attitude to the world? The optimists of his day said that the world was good and getting better, and that we should be content with it. The pessimists said that the world was bad, and that the wise man despises it. Chesterton found that neither attitude was right, and that both were, in different ways, inhuman. His answer, in the chapter called The Flag of the World, is one of his most original contributions to Christian thought.

Not optimism but patriotism

Our attitude to the world, he argued, ought not to be that of a critic weighing up a hotel, deciding whether its rooms are good enough to stay in. It ought to be more like the loyalty of a man to his own home or country. “My acceptance of the universe is not optimism,” he wrote, “it is more like patriotism.” A man does not love his home because it is the best home in the world. He loves it because it is his, and because he loves it he wants to make it better. If it is falling down, he does not leave; he repairs it.

This, Chesterton saw, solves the old riddle of how a man can both love the world and want to change it. The optimist loves it too little to see what is wrong with it; the pessimist sees what is wrong with it but does not love it enough to mend it. The patriot does both. He illustrated the point with Rome. The city, he said, did not become great and then win the love of its people. It was loved first, and its greatness grew from that love. “Men did not love Rome because she was great,” he wrote. “She was great because they had loved her.”

But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us. ROMANS 5:8

The Christian will see at once that this is a picture of how God loves the world. He did not love it because it was lovely. He loved it while it was ruined, and His love was the beginning of its renewal.

Loving the world, hating its sin

Chesterton found the Christian faith fitted this attitude exactly, and for a reason that surprised him. The optimists of his day had tried to make people happy by telling them that they fitted into the world, that man was simply one animal among others, at home in nature. But Chesterton had never felt at home in that way. The Christian account, he discovered, explained why. Man does not fit into the world as it now is, because he was made for a better one, and the world has fallen from what it was meant to be. The Christian may love the world as God made it, and hate with all his heart what sin has done to it, without contradiction.

For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now. ROMANS 8:22

The martyr and the suicide

In the same chapter Chesterton wrote some of his sternest pages, on suicide. He had been near enough to despair in his youth to know its pull, and he believed the fashionable pessimism of his day was making it seem noble. He would have none of it. The man who takes his own life, he said, does not merely end one life; as far as he is concerned, he refuses the whole world. And he set beside him the martyr, who also dies, but for the opposite reason: not because he despises life, but because he loves something more than his own life. The two deaths look alike from outside and are utterly opposed. The church, he said, had always marked the difference.

These pages are severe, and some readers who have lost loved ones in this way may find them hard. It should be said plainly that Chesterton was writing against an idea — the glorification of despair — and not passing judgement on the suffering people who are overwhelmed by it. Despair is a terrible enemy, and those who are caught by it need not condemnation but help, and the hope of the gospel.

I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life. DEUTERONOMY 30:19

Weighing it

Chesterton’s cosmic patriotism is a precious idea, and it guards the Christian against two opposite errors: the worldliness that loves the world as it is, and the false spirituality that despises the world God made. It fits the Bible’s story — a good creation, a terrible fall, a loving God who does not abandon what He made.

fields.title: The Furious Opposites
fields.body_html:
Mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other. PSALM 85:10

The chapter of Orthodoxy called The Paradoxes of Christianity is the hinge of the whole book, and it begins with Chesterton’s own puzzlement. As a young man, still outside the faith, he had read a great deal of anti-Christian writing, by the famous sceptics of his day. And the more he read, the more he noticed something odd. The critics of Christianity did not agree about what was wrong with it. Indeed, they contradicted each other flatly.

Attacked from every side

One critic said that Christianity was too gloomy, a religion of monks and funerals that had taken the joy out of life. Another said that it was too cheerful, a comfortable fairy tale that hid from men the real misery of the world. One said that it was too meek, teaching men to submit to tyranny and turn the other cheek; another that it was too warlike, the cause of crusades and persecutions. One said that it despised women by its monks and celibates; another that it pampered them, filling the churches with them. One said that it was the enemy of the family; another that it was the family’s narrowest defender.

At first this simply confirmed his unbelief. Surely a religion attacked from every direction must be very bad indeed. But slowly another thought dawned on him. If a man is called too fat by one critic and too thin by another, it may be that he is very oddly shaped. But it may also be that he is exactly the right shape, and that his critics are the odd ones. Perhaps Christianity was not a monstrosity at all. Perhaps it was the only sane thing in the room, and each critic was measuring it by his own particular madness.

Keeping both furious

As Chesterton looked more closely, he found that this was exactly the case. Christianity had a habit, not of finding a comfortable middle point between two virtues, but of holding both of them at full strength at once. He took courage as his first example. True courage, he said, is a kind of contradiction: it means a strong desire to live, taking the form of a readiness to die. The soldier surrounded by enemies will escape only if he fights his way out with a reckless disregard for his life. He must, in a phrase from this chapter, “desire life like water and yet drink death like wine.” Christianity, Chesterton found, had not watered down either desire. It had kept both.

For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. MATTHEW 16:25

So it was with humility and dignity. The pagan world had tried to find a balance: a man should think moderately well of himself, neither too proud nor too humble. Christianity did something far stranger. It told a man that he was a miserable sinner, utterly unworthy, and at the same time that he was a creature of infinite worth for whom the Son of God had died. Chesterton summed up the whole pattern in a single sentence: “Christianity got over the difficulty of combining furious opposites, by keeping them both, and keeping them both furious.” And of humility and dignity in particular: “One can hardly think too little of one’s self. One can hardly think too much of one’s soul.”

I am a worm, and no man. PSALM 22:6
Ye are bought with a price. 1 CORINTHIANS 7:23

It was the same with mercy and judgement. The Christian is to be far angrier at sin than the pagan ever was, and far kinder to the sinner. It was the same with the church’s love of the world and its call to renounce it, with its pageantry and its poverty, its saints in sackcloth and its cathedrals in gold. Chesterton concluded that the church had not compromised between these things but set them side by side, each in its full colour, like the red and white upon the shield of St George, rather than mixing them into pink. “The more I considered Christianity,” he wrote, “the more I found that while it had established a rule and order, the chief aim of that order was to give room for good things to run wild.”

The God-Man

Chesterton saw that this pattern was no accident. It runs back to the centre of the faith. At the heart of the creed stands a Person who is not half God and half man, a sort of compromise between the two, but fully God and fully man at once. The church did not split the difference between His divinity and His humanity. It held both, without diminishing either. All the other paradoxes, Chesterton thought, are echoes of that one.

And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory. 1 TIMOTHY 3:16

Why an inch matters

This, he argued, explains something that sceptics have always found absurd about the history of the church: its fierce quarrels over apparently tiny points of doctrine. Why should the councils have argued for years over a single letter in a Greek word? Because, Chesterton answered, when you are holding a great balance, an inch is everything. If the church had let go of Christ’s divinity, or of His humanity, the whole structure would have toppled, and with it everything that made the faith the faith. The councils were not quibbling. They were keeping their balance on a tightrope.

Weighing it

This is one of the most illuminating chapters in all of Chesterton, and much of it can be received without reserve. The Bible is full of the furious opposites he described: the Lord who is a lion and a lamb, the gospel that humbles and exalts, the God who is just and the justifier of him that believeth.

To declare, I say, at this time his righteousness: that he might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus. ROMANS 3:26

Two cautions are in order. First, the word paradox can become an excuse. Chesterton used it to describe truths that look contradictory but are not, because Scripture teaches both. It is not a licence to call any confusion a mystery or to believe two genuinely contradictory things. The test is always whether both sides are written.

Second, when Chesterton describes the church as holding all these opposites, he is thinking of the visible church of history, with its monasteries and its pageantry, and in later life he identified that church with Rome. Evangelical readers will believe that the balance he loved is found first in Scripture itself, and that the visible churches, Rome included, have often lost it. The cure for an unbalanced church is not a greater confidence in the church, but a closer reading of the Bible.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Which of the furious opposites do you find hardest to hold together: humility and dignity, wrath at sin and mercy to sinners, love of the world and renunciation of it?

2. Have you watered down one of them to make the other easier? Ask God to restore it.

3. Read Philippians 2:5–11 and notice the paradox at the centre of the faith: the God who humbled Himself and was highly exalted.

4. Think of a doctrine you have dismissed as a quibble. Ask what might fall if it were let go.

5. Read the chapter of Orthodoxy called The Paradoxes of Christianity, in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, You are the Lion and the Lamb, truly God and truly man.
I confess that I am less than nothing in myself, and I thank You that You thought me worth dying for.
Make me angrier at sin and kinder to sinners. Make me love Your world and hold it loosely.
Keep me balanced on the narrow way, not by my own skill, but by holding fast to You. Amen.

fields.title: The Wild Truth Reeling but Erect
fields.body_html:
Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints. JUDE 3

Most people of Chesterton’s day, and most of ours, thought of orthodoxy as a dull thing: safe, heavy, respectable, the opposite of adventure. Heresy, by contrast, seemed bold and exciting, the mark of a free mind. Orthodoxy is the book in which Chesterton turned that picture upside down. The two chapters at the heart of its argument, The Paradoxes of Christianity and The Romance of Orthodoxy, set out to show that the true faith is the most thrilling thing in the world, and heresy the most tame.

The heavenly chariot

At the close of the chapter on paradox, Chesterton painted a picture that has stayed with his readers ever since. Orthodoxy, he said, is not a resting-place but a balancing act. There are a thousand ways of falling and only one way of standing upright. To have fallen into any one of the errors that have tempted the church — from the ancient Gnostics to the fashionable sects of his own day — would have been easy and dull. To have avoided all of them, century after century, was a breathless adventure. He imagined it as a chariot racing through history: “in my vision the heavenly chariot flies thundering through the ages, the dull heresies sprawling and prostrate, the wild truth reeling but erect.”

Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. PSALM 119:105

The picture is worth dwelling on, because it changes the way a Christian thinks about doctrine. The creeds are not walls built to keep thought in. They are the record of a narrow road, kept open at great cost, between dangers on either side. To deny the deity of Christ is easy; to deny His humanity is easy; to hold both is hard and glorious. Every heresy is a simplification, and every simplification is a fall.

The freedom of dogma

In The Romance of Orthodoxy Chesterton went further. The liberal theologians of his time claimed that by abandoning the old doctrines they were making Christianity more free. Chesterton argued that the reverse was true. Take away the doctrine that God is distinct from His creation, and you are left with a God who is simply the universe — and a man who worships the universe has no ground for resisting anything in it. Take away the doctrine of the fall, and you lose the right to call anything a corruption that needs reforming. Take away miracles, and you have a universe locked shut against God. Take away the Trinity, and you have a God who is a solitary power rather than an eternal fellowship of love. Each of the old dogmas, he said, turned out to be the guarantee of some freedom that the moderns valued.

If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed. JOHN 8:36

He gave a picture for this too, in the last chapter of the book. Imagine children playing on the flat grassy top of a tall island in the sea. As long as there is a wall around the edge, they can run and play and fling themselves about in safety. Take the wall away, and they will huddle in the middle, afraid of the drop. Doctrine, he said, is that wall. It does not end the game; it makes the game possible.

Always a revolution

In the chapter between these two, The Eternal Revolution, Chesterton made a related point about progress. Everyone in his day talked about progress, but progress means moving towards something, and you cannot move towards a goal that keeps changing. A people that alters its ideal every generation is not progressing; it is merely drifting. The Christian has a fixed ideal, given by God and seen in Christ, and because it is fixed he can always measure the world against it and find it wanting. That, Chesterton said, is why the Christian is always a reformer, and why the doctrine of original sin, far from making men content with injustice, is the strongest of all grounds for fighting it.

In the same chapter comes a light-hearted sentence that says something serious about the Christian life: “Angels can fly because they can take themselves lightly.” The saints, he observed, have been marked not by solemnity about themselves but by a holy levity — a freedom from self-importance that comes from knowing that everything rests on God.

Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you. 1 PETER 5:7

Weighing it

Chesterton’s vision of orthodoxy as adventure is a gift to every generation of believers, and especially to young believers who have been told that faith is the enemy of thought. He was right that heresy is usually dull, that the creeds guard a narrow and exhilarating road, and that dogma is a defence of freedom rather than an attack on it.

The caution concerns who keeps the road. When Chesterton speaks of orthodoxy he means the faith of the creeds, and evangelical readers can stand with him there. But his chariot is driven, in his imagination, by the church; and when he later became a Catholic he came to believe that the Roman Church’s teaching authority was the means by which God had kept the truth from falling. Evangelicals believe that the truth has been kept by God’s Word, and that churches, Rome included, have sometimes fallen off the road and needed Scripture to set them back on it. The Reformation itself was one such recovery. The faith once delivered to the saints is the standard by which every church is tested.

To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them. ISAIAH 8:20
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Have you thought of orthodoxy as safe and dull? How does Chesterton’s picture of the chariot change that?

2. Read the Nicene Creed slowly, and for each line ask what would be lost if it were denied.

3. Is there a doctrine that you have found confining? Consider whether it might be a wall that makes the playground safe.

4. Where are you taking yourself too seriously? Practise casting one care on God this week.

5. Read the chapter of Orthodoxy called The Romance of Orthodoxy, in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Lord, You have given Your church the faith once for all delivered to the saints, and You have kept it through every age.
Forgive me for thinking Your truth dull, and for being dazzled by errors that are only simplifications.
Keep me on the narrow road between the dangers on either side, and let Your Word be a lamp to my feet.
Make me light-hearted about myself and earnest about Your truth, and give me the joy of the adventure, for Jesus’ sake. Amen.

Doctrine, he said, is that wall. It does not end the game; it makes the game possible. Everyone in his day talked about progress, but progress means moving towards something, and you cannot move towards a goal that keeps changing. A people that alters its ideal every generation is not progressing; it is merely drifting. The Christian has a fixed ideal, given by God and seen in Christ, and because it is fixed he can always measure the world against it and find it wanting. That, Chesterton said, is why the Christian is always a reformer, and why the doctrine of original sin, far from making men content with injustice, is the strongest of all grounds for fighting it. Evangelicals believe that the truth has been kept by God’s Word, and that churches, Rome included, have sometimes fallen off the road and needed Scripture to set them back on it. The Reformation itself was one such recovery. The faith once delivered to the saints is the standard by which every church is tested. To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them. ISAIAH 8:20 FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Have you thought of orthodoxy as safe and dull? How does Chesterton’s picture of the chariot change that? 2. Read the Nicene Creed slowly, and for each line ask what would be lost if it were denied. 3. Is there a doctrine that you have found confining? Consider whether it might be a wall that makes the playground safe. 4. Where are you taking yourself too seriously? Practise casting one care on God this week. 5. Read the chapter of Orthodoxy called The Romance of Orthodoxy, in the Ochorus library. Forgive me for thinking Your truth dull, and for being dazzled by errors that are only simplifications. Keep me on the narrow road between the dangers on either side, and let Your Word be a lamp to my feet. Make me light-hearted about myself and earnest about Your truth, and give me the joy of the adventure, for Jesus’ sake. Amen.

fields.title: The Gigantic Secret
fields.body_html:
These things have I spoken unto you, that my joy might remain in you, and that your joy might be full. JOHN 15:11

Orthodoxy ends with joy. Its last pages are among the most beautiful Chesterton ever wrote, and they contain the sentence by which, more than any other, he is remembered. He had spent the book showing that Christianity was true and sane. He closed it by showing that it was glad.

The small publicity and the gigantic secret

The pagan world, Chesterton said, had been joyful in small things and sad in great ones. The ancient Greek could enjoy the wine and the dance and the sunlight, but when he looked at the ultimate questions — death, fate, the meaning of the whole — he saw only darkness and doom. His joy was on the surface; his grief was at the root. Christianity reversed this. The Christian may weep over many small things in this world, for it is fallen and full of sorrow, but at the root of everything he knows that all is well, that God is good, that death is defeated and that love will have the last word. The Christian’s grief is on the surface; his joy is at the root.

Chesterton put it in the famous sentence from the chapter called Authority and the Adventurer: “Joy, which was the small publicity of the pagan, is the gigantic secret of the Christian.”

As sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing; as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing all things. 2 CORINTHIANS 6:10

Joy as the heart of the universe

He believed that this was not merely a feeling, but a fact about the world. Joy, not sorrow, is the deepest thing in reality, because God Himself is joyful. Sorrow is real, but it is a parenthesis. The story of the world is a comedy, in the old sense of a story with a happy ending, and the believer may laugh at the end of it because he knows how it ends.

Weeping may endure for a night, but joy cometh in the morning. PSALM 30:5

The mirth of Christ

And then, in the very last paragraph of the book, Chesterton turned to the Gospels. He noticed that the Christ of the Gospels is a figure of enormous emotion. He weeps; He is angry; He is moved with compassion; He speaks with a fierceness that terrified the religious leaders of His day. He did not hide His tears or His wrath. But there was something, Chesterton suggested, that He did hide — something that He kept to Himself when He went up a mountain alone to pray. “There was some one thing that was too great for God to show us when He walked upon our earth,” he wrote, “and I have sometimes fancied that it was His mirth.”

It is a daring thought, and Chesterton offered it as a fancy, not a doctrine. But it rests on something real. The Gospels speak of Christ’s joy, and the epistles speak of a joy set before Him that carried Him through the cross itself.

Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God. HEBREWS 12:2
In that hour Jesus rejoiced in spirit, and said, I thank thee, O Father, Lord of heaven and earth. LUKE 10:21

Joy and holiness

Chesterton never thought that joy was a substitute for holiness, or that the Christian should be cheerful in a shallow, bouncing way. He knew sorrow; he had nearly lost his mind, his health and his brother. His joy was not the absence of pain but the deep conviction underneath it. And it was, he thought, one of the great evidences of the faith. A religion that was false would have to make its followers either grim or giddy. Christianity made them glad.

Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice. PHILIPPIANS 4:4

Weighing it

This is Chesterton at his best and most biblical. The New Testament is a book of joy, and the believer’s joy is a fruit of the Spirit and a command of God. Much modern Christianity, earnest and anxious, needs to hear it.

One caution is worth adding. Chesterton’s fancy about the hidden mirth of Christ is beautiful and reverent, but it is a fancy, and he said so. Scripture tells us that Christ was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief, and that His joy was a joy that passed through the cross. The Christian’s joy is not a temperament but a gift; it flows not from a cheerful disposition but from the finished work of the Saviour. Chesterton’s own exuberance was a natural gift as well as a grace, and believers of a quieter temperament should not think themselves less joyful because they laugh less loudly. The joy of the Lord is their strength too.

He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief. ISAIAH 53:3
The joy of the Lord is your strength. NEHEMIAH 8:10
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Is your joy on the surface and your grief at the root, or the other way round? What would it take to reverse it?

2. Read Philippians, the epistle of joy, in one sitting, and note every mention of rejoicing.

3. Read Hebrews 12:1–3 and consider the joy that was set before Christ.

4. Think of a sorrow you are carrying. Bring it to God, and ask Him to show you the joy beneath it.

5. Read the closing pages of Orthodoxy, the chapter called Authority and the Adventurer, in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You were a man of sorrows, and You endured the cross for the joy that was set before You.
Thank You that sorrow is not the deepest thing in the world, and that joy will have the last word.
Where my grief has gone down to the root, plant Your joy beneath it. Where my joy has been shallow, make it deep.
Let my life be a witness to the gigantic secret, that in You all is well, and all shall be well for ever. Amen.

fields.title: The Democracy of the Dead
fields.body_html:
For enquire, I pray thee, of the former age, and prepare thyself to the search of their fathers: for we are but of yesterday, and know nothing. JOB 8:8–9

Chesterton called himself a democrat all his life, and he meant it. He believed that the ordinary man’s instincts about the great things of life — love, birth, death, home, God — were more trustworthy than the theories of the clever. In The Ethics of Elfland he stated his democratic creed in two parts. The first was “that the things common to all men are more important than the things peculiar to any men.” The second was that the ordinary man should be trusted with the most important things, such as choosing his own government or falling in love, rather than having them decided for him by experts. From this he drew a conclusion that surprised his readers.

Votes for our ancestors

If we trust the opinion of ordinary men when they agree in great numbers today, he asked, why should we not trust their opinion when they agreed in great numbers yesterday, and the day before, and for a thousand years? The modern habit was to treat the beliefs of the past as automatically out of date, simply because they were old. Chesterton thought this was a kind of snobbery — a snobbery of time, which disqualifies men by the accident of when they were born, as the old aristocrats disqualified them by the accident of birth.

He put it, in the same chapter, in a paragraph that has become one of his most famous: “Tradition means giving votes to the most obscure of all classes, our ancestors. It is the democracy of the dead. Tradition refuses to submit to the small and arrogant oligarchy of those who merely happen to be walking about.”

One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts. PSALM 145:4

Why tradition matters to the Christian

This is more than a clever saying. It goes to the heart of how Christians receive their faith. No believer starts from nothing. We learn the gospel from those who learned it before us, and they from others, back to the apostles who were eyewitnesses of Christ. Scripture itself commands the passing on of the faith from one generation to the next, and it warns against a restless craving for novelty.

And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also. 2 TIMOTHY 2:2
Remove not the ancient landmark, which thy fathers have set. PROVERBS 22:28

Chesterton’s point was that the great Christian consensus — the creeds, the shared convictions of believers across the centuries — deserves a hearing that the latest fashion does not. A belief held by Augustine and Aquinas, by Luther and Wesley, by countless unnamed believers in every land and century, is not refuted because a lecturer in London finds it unfashionable.

The fence in the field

He made the same point in a later book, The Thing (1929), with a famous parable, about a reformer who comes upon a fence or a gate across a road and wants to clear it away, because he can see no use for it. The wiser man tells him that he must first go and find out why it was put there; only when he knows its purpose may he decide whether to take it down. The parable is a plea not against change but against careless change: the institutions and customs we inherit were usually built for a reason, and the reason should be understood before they are destroyed.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21

Weighing it

There is great wisdom here, and evangelical readers, who are sometimes too quick to treat everything before the last revival as irrelevant, need to hear it. The church did not begin with us, and we are foolish if we ignore the saints who have gone before.

But a careful distinction is needed. For Chesterton, especially in his later years, tradition came to carry an authority alongside Scripture, as the Roman Catholic Church teaches: the living voice of the church interpreting and, in effect, adding to the written Word. Evangelical Christians honour tradition, but they place it under Scripture, not beside it. The fathers and the creeds are precious because, and in so far as, they are faithful to the Bible. Jesus Himself rebuked the religious leaders of His day for allowing their traditions to override the commandment of God.

Thus have ye made the commandment of God of none effect by your tradition. MATTHEW 15:6

The democracy of the dead is a wise principle for weighing human opinions. But the Word of God is not one voice among the voters. It is the law by which the votes are counted.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Have you dismissed a belief simply because it was old? Consider whether it was ever actually refuted.

2. Name three Christians from earlier centuries whose faith has shaped yours. Thank God for them.

3. Read Psalm 78:1–8 and notice how the faith is passed from one generation to the next.

4. Is there a fence in your life — a habit, a custom, a rule — that you are tempted to tear down? Find out first why it was put there.

5. Read Matthew 15:1–9 and ask where your own traditions may have crept above God’s Word.

A PRAYER
Lord, You have been the dwelling place of Your people in all generations.
Thank You for the saints who kept the faith and handed it on to me, through dark centuries and bright ones.
Keep me from the pride that thinks my own age wiser than all others, and from the folly that tears down what it does not understand.
Above all, keep me under Your Word, by which every tradition is tested, and let me hand on the faith faithfully to those who come after me. Amen.
