fields.title: Humility in the Right Place
fields.body_html:
Not unto us, O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory, for thy mercy, and for thy truth’s sake. PSALM 115:1

Chesterton was one of the most famous men in England, and one of the least vain. Those who knew him remarked again and again on his lack of self-importance. He laughed at himself more readily than at anyone else, and he called Orthodoxy a joke at his own expense. It is fitting that one of his most enduring contributions to Christian thought should be about humility.

The fool of the story

He began Orthodoxy by laughing at himself. He had set out, he said, as a young man determined to be original, to think his way to a new philosophy that no one had ever discovered. And he found, to his great embarrassment, that he had arrived at Christianity: the oldest and most commonplace creed in England. He compared himself to an English yachtsman who sets out to discover a new island in the South Seas and lands, with great ceremony, at Brighton. “I am the man who with the utmost daring discovered what had been discovered before,” he wrote, in the chapter called Introduction in Defence of Everything Else.

That is a picture of humility, and a very Christian one. The truth was not his invention. He had not added to it. He had simply been brought, by a long and comic road, to the place where countless ordinary believers had been standing all along.

What hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it? 1 CORINTHIANS 4:7

The wrong kind and the right kind

As we have seen, Chesterton believed that his age had put humility in the wrong place. It was humble about truth, which it hardly dared claim to know, and proud about the self, which it trusted without question. He wanted it the other way round. True humility, as the Christian tradition understood it, means a low view of one’s own importance joined to a high confidence in the truth of God. The humble man is not the one who says that nobody can know anything. He is the one who knows that he himself is small, and that God is great, and says so.

God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble. JAMES 4:6

Humility and wonder

Chesterton saw a close link between humility and the wonder he prized so much. The proud man, he thought, cannot enjoy anything, because he thinks he deserves everything. Nothing surprises him, because he takes it all as his due. The humble man, by contrast, receives everything as a gift, and so everything delights him. In this sense humility is the secret of joy. It is the small person who finds the world large, and the person who expects nothing who is astonished by everything.

He loved to say, in many places and many ways, that the man who thinks of himself as a creature, small before an immense God, finds the world full of giants and wonders; while the man who makes himself the centre finds the world dwindling to the size of his own mind. This is why the saints have so often been the happiest of people.

Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. MATTHEW 5:3

Humility in argument

Chesterton’s humility showed itself most clearly in the way he argued. He fought hard, and he was formidable in debate, but he never seemed to want to humiliate his opponents. He believed they were wrong; he never believed they were worthless. He kept friendships with men who disagreed with him about everything that mattered, and he was quick to praise what was good in their work even as he attacked what was false. That combination — certainty about the truth and charity towards persons — is exactly what he meant by humility in the right place.

And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. 2 TIMOTHY 2:24–25

Weighing it

Chesterton’s teaching on humility is wise and biblical, and his own example gives it weight. Few teachers have shown so clearly that a man can be both certain and gentle.

Two things may be added. The first is that the root of Christian humility is not finally the smallness of man before the size of the universe, true as that is, but the sinfulness of man before the holiness of God, and the mercy shown to him at the cross. Chesterton knew this, and said it often enough. But a reader who takes from him only a cheerful sense of his own littleness has missed the deepest humbling of all, which is to be forgiven.

But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world. GALATIANS 6:14

The second is that Chesterton’s charity in argument did not always reach as far as it should. As we noted at the start of this book, there were people about whom he wrote without charity, and the Jewish people were among them. His own principle condemns those pages: a man who is certain of the truth and humble about himself has no room for contempt of his neighbour.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where are you proud about yourself and timid about the truth? Where are you humble in the wrong place?

2. Think of something you are tempted to take credit for. Read 1 Corinthians 4:7 and give the credit back to God.

3. List three things that have surprised and delighted you this week. Notice the link between gratitude and humility.

4. Think of someone with whom you strongly disagree. Pray for them by name, and look for something good in them to thank God for.

5. Read the opening chapter of Orthodoxy, Introduction in Defence of Everything Else, in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Lord, not unto us, but unto Your name be the glory.
Forgive me for being proud of what I have received, and for being afraid to confess what You have revealed.
Make me small in my own eyes and bold in Your truth, gentle with those who oppose me and grateful for every gift.
Humble me at the cross, where my pride was answered and my sin forgiven, and let me glory in nothing else. Amen.

That is a picture of humility, and a very Christian one. The truth was not his invention. He had not added to it. He had simply been brought, by a long and comic road, to the place where countless ordinary believers had been standing all along. What hast thou that thou didst not receive? now if thou didst receive it, why dost thou glory, as if thou hadst not received it? 1 CORINTHIANS 4:7 The wrong kind and the right kind As we have seen, Chesterton believed that his age had put humility in the wrong place. It was humble about truth, which it hardly dared claim to know, and proud about the self, which it trusted without question. He wanted it the other way round. True humility, as the Christian tradition understood it, means a low view of one’s own importance joined to a high confidence in the truth of God. The humble man is not the one who says that nobody can know anything. He is the one who knows that he himself is small, and that God is great, and says so. God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble. JAMES 4:6 Humility and wonder Chesterton saw a close link between humility and the wonder he prized so much. The proud man, he thought, cannot enjoy anything, because he thinks he deserves everything. Nothing surprises him, because he takes it all as his due. The humble man, by contrast, receives everything as a gift, and so everything delights him. In this sense humility is the secret of joy. It is the small person who finds the world large, and the person who expects nothing who is astonished by everything. He loved to say, in many places and many ways, that the man who thinks of himself as a creature, small before an immense God, finds the world full of giants and wonders; while the man who makes himself the centre finds the world dwindling to the size of his own mind. This is why the saints have so often been the happiest of people. Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. He fought hard, and he was formidable in debate, but he never seemed to want to humiliate his opponents. He believed they were wrong; he never believed they were worthless. He kept friendships with men who disagreed with him about everything that mattered, and he was quick to praise what was good in their work even as he attacked what was false. That combination — certainty about the truth and charity towards persons — is exactly what he meant by humility in the right place. And the servant of the Lord must not strive; but be gentle unto all men, apt to teach, patient, in meekness instructing those that oppose themselves. 2 TIMOTHY 2:24–25 Weighing it Chesterton’s teaching on humility is wise and biblical, and his own example gives it weight. Few teachers have shown so clearly that a man can be both certain and gentle. Two things may be added. The first is that the root of Christian humility is not finally the smallness of man before the size of the universe, true as that is, but the sinfulness of man before the holiness of God, and the mercy shown to him at the cross. Chesterton knew this, and said it often enough. But a reader who takes from him only a cheerful sense of his own littleness has missed the deepest humbling of all, which is to be forgiven. But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world. As we noted at the start of this book, there were people about whom he wrote without charity, and the Jewish people were among them. His own principle condemns those pages: a man who is certain of the truth and humble about himself has no room for contempt of his neighbour. FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION 1. Where are you proud about yourself and timid about the truth? Where are you humble in the wrong place? 2. Think of something you are tempted to take credit for. Read 1 Corinthians 4:7 and give the credit back to God. 3. List three things that have surprised and delighted you this week. Notice the link between gratitude and humility. 4. Think of someone with whom you strongly disagree. Pray for them by name, and look for something good in them to thank God for. 5. Read the opening chapter of Orthodoxy, Introduction in Defence of Everything Else, in the Ochorus library. A PRAYER Lord, not unto us, but unto Your name be the glory. Forgive me for being proud of what I have received, and for being afraid to confess what You have revealed. Make me small in my own eyes and bold in Your truth, gentle with those who oppose me and grateful for every gift. Humble me at the cross, where my pride was answered and my sin forgiven, and let me glory in nothing else. Amen.

fields.title: The Dignity of Ordinary Things
fields.body_html:
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. COLOSSIANS 3:23

If Chesterton had a single social conviction, it was that ordinary life is sacred. He loved the common man — not the abstract worker of the economists or the voter of the politicians, but the actual man in the street, with his family, his house, his pint of beer, his small garden and his large opinions. He believed that the things such a man cares about most — his wife and children, his home, his freedom, his faith — are the most important things in the world, and that every theory which belittles them is wrong.

More extraordinary than the extraordinary

In The Ethics of Elfland he stated the principle with a characteristic twist. The things common to all men, he said, matter more than the things peculiar to any; and then: “Ordinary things are more valuable than extraordinary things; nay, they are more extraordinary.” Birth, marriage, the raising of a child, the sharing of a meal, the death of an old man in his own bed: these are not dull because they are common. They are common because they are so tremendously important that every human being must take part in them.

This gave Chesterton a deep respect for the home. He thought that the family was the one truly free institution left in the modern world — the one place where a man and a woman could build something of their own, by their own rules, under no master but God. He defended it against the reformers of his day who wanted to hand more and more of its work to the state or the factory. He defended marriage, too, as a lifelong vow, and wrote a short book in its defence against the loosening of the divorce laws.

Except the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. PSALM 127:1

The holiness of small things

The Christian will see the biblical root of this. The God of the Bible is the God of ordinary life. He appears to shepherds at their work and fishermen at their nets. He commands that the Sabbath be kept in every household, that bread be shared with the hungry, that children be taught the faith as they sit at home and walk by the way. The incarnation itself is the supreme dignifying of ordinary things: the Son of God spent thirty years in a village workshop before He preached a single sermon.

Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary? MARK 6:3

Chesterton took this seriously. He believed that the housewife and the craftsman, the small farmer and the shopkeeper, were doing work of immense dignity, and that a civilisation which forgot it was in danger.

Three acres and a cow

From this conviction grew his politics. With his friend Hilaire Belloc, Chesterton championed what came to be called distributism. They were equally suspicious of big business and of big government. Capitalism, as they saw it, concentrated property in the hands of a few rich men, so that most people owned nothing and worked for wages; socialism concentrated it in the hands of the state, which was no better. Their alternative was to distribute property as widely as possible, so that as many families as possible owned the land they farmed, the shop they kept or the tools they worked with. They made their own an older slogan of English land reformers: three acres and a cow. Chesterton set out the case in The Outline of Sanity (1926) and promoted it in G. K.’s Weekly, and in 1926 he and his friends founded the Distributist League.

But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid. MICAH 4:4

Weighing it

Much in this chapter will warm evangelical hearts. Chesterton’s love of the home, his defence of marriage, his respect for ordinary work and his suspicion of anything that treats human beings as cogs in a machine are deeply Christian instincts, and they have aged well. The Reformation itself taught that the farmer and the housewife serve God as truly as the monk.

But distributism must be weighed for what it is. It is an economic opinion, and a disputed one. Chesterton held it with passion, and he sometimes wrote as though it followed directly from the faith. It does not. Scripture certainly teaches the dignity of work, the duty of the rich to the poor, the evil of oppression and the goodness of private property; it does not prescribe a particular economic system, and Christians who share every article of Chesterton’s creed have held every kind of view about how those principles are best served. Distributism also drew much of its inspiration from Roman Catholic social teaching, which evangelicals may admire without treating as binding. The same caution applies to many of his political opinions, on the Boer War, on Irish home rule, on women’s suffrage and on much else: they are the views of a vigorous journalist, often wise and sometimes not, but they are not the gospel.

Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s. MATTHEW 22:21

The reader should take from Chesterton his love of ordinary things and his concern for the poor, and think for himself, with Scripture open, about the economics.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. What ordinary thing in your life — a meal, a household task, a daily walk — have you treated as dull? Offer it to God as worship this week.

2. Read Deuteronomy 6:4–9 and notice how ordinary home life becomes the place where the faith is taught.

3. Thank God for the carpenter’s years at Nazareth, and for the dignity they give to ordinary work.

4. Is your home a place of freedom and love, or merely a place where people sleep? Consider one step towards making it more of a home.

5. Think about one economic or political opinion you hold strongly. Ask yourself honestly whether it is a conviction of Scripture or an opinion of your own.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, You worked with Your hands at Nazareth, and You made ordinary things holy.
Thank You for my home and my work, my daily bread and the people I share it with.
Teach me to do every small task heartily, as to You, and to see the glory in common things.
Give me a heart for the poor and the powerless, and wisdom to serve them well, and keep me from mistaking my own opinions for Your word. Amen.

fields.title: The Man in the Cave
fields.body_html:
So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them. GENESIS 1:27

In 1920 H. G. Wells published The Outline of History, a vast and enormously popular account of the human story from the beginning of the universe to the Great War. Its message, broadly, was that man is an animal who has gradually evolved, that religion is one of the stages through which he has passed, and that Jesus was a remarkable teacher among many. Chesterton, who liked Wells and disagreed with him about almost everything, set out to tell the same story the other way round. The result was The Everlasting Man (1925), which many readers think his greatest book. Its first part is about man; its second is about Christ.

Seeing it from outside

Chesterton began with an unusual claim. In his introduction he wrote that “the next best thing to being really inside Christendom is to be really outside it.” His complaint about the critics of Christianity was that they were neither: they were too familiar with it to see it, and too hostile to understand it. His aim, therefore, was to make the familiar strange again — to look at man, and at Christ, as though for the first time, with the eyes of someone who had never heard the story before.

The picture on the wall

He started in a cave. He imagined a priest and a boy crawling through a long tunnel in the hills and coming out, at last, in a cavern on whose walls, by lamplight, they see the paintings left there by prehistoric men: great sprawling outlines of reindeer and horses and bison, drawn with skill and life. Such caves had indeed been discovered not long before he wrote.

What does the boy learn from the paintings? Not, Chesterton said, that the men who made them were brutes. He learns the opposite: that they were men, very like ourselves, with the very human urge to make pictures. And then he notices something so simple that it is easily missed. He has found the place where a man drew a picture of a reindeer. He would have to dig a great deal deeper before he found the place where a reindeer drew a picture of a man. In the chapter called The Man in the Cave Chesterton put the conclusion in five words: “Art is the signature of man.”

I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well. PSALM 139:14

Different in kind

This is the argument of the whole first part of the book. Man is an animal, but he is not merely an animal. He is different from every other creature, not in degree but in kind. No other creature paints, or prays, or buries its dead with ceremony, or tells stories, or laughs, or asks what it is for. The more closely we look at man as an animal, Chesterton said, the stranger he appears. In the same chapter: “the more we really look at man as an animal, the less he will look like one.”

He went on, through the following chapters, to look at the earliest civilisations, the religions and mythologies of the ancient world, and the philosophies of Greece and India, and he argued that in each of them the same thing appears: a creature haunted by the sense of something beyond the world, reaching out in myth and ritual and thought towards a God he could not quite find. The myths were dreams, he said; the philosophies were guesses; and the whole of the ancient world was waiting.

That they should seek the Lord, if haply they might feel after him, and find him, though he be not far from every one of us. ACTS 17:27

Weighing it

Chesterton’s account of the uniqueness of man is a powerful and much-needed answer to the belief that human beings are nothing but clever animals. It stands on the first chapter of Genesis: man alone is made in the image of God, and the marks of that image — creativity, reason, worship, moral sense — are everywhere visible, even in the oldest traces of human life.

Two points may be weighed. First, Chesterton was not arguing against every theory of biological development; he was arguing against the philosophy, often attached to it, which says that man is merely a product of nature with no more meaning than a beetle. He was content to leave the scientific details to the scientists, and his own views on them were not those of every evangelical reader. What he insisted on was that, however the human body came to be, the human being is something new in the world, and points beyond the world.

Second, his account of the pagan myths as dreams and guesses, reaching out towards the truth, is generous and often illuminating. But Scripture also speaks more darkly of the religions of the nations, as the worship of creatures in place of the Creator. Chesterton knew this, and he wrote of the dark side of paganism with real horror in later chapters. The reader should hold both truths: that the human heart was made for God and seeks Him, and that left to itself it turns that seeking into idolatry.

And changed the glory of the uncorruptible God into an image made like to corruptible man, and to birds, and fourfooted beasts, and creeping things. ROMANS 1:23
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Think of the things that you do that no animal does: pray, create, laugh, grieve, ask questions. Thank God for His image in you.

2. Read Psalm 8 and Genesis 1:26–31 slowly, and consider what it means to be made in God’s image.

3. Consider someone you find hard to respect. Remember that they too bear God’s image.

4. Read Acts 17:22–31 and notice how Paul speaks to people who were feeling after God.

5. Read the chapter of The Everlasting Man called The Man in the Cave, in the Ochorus library.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You made man in Your own image, and You crowned him with glory and honour.
Thank You that I am not merely an animal, but a creature made to know You, to praise You and to make things for Your glory.
Forgive me for the times I have lived beneath my calling, and treated others as less than Your image-bearers.
Thank You that what the ancient world reached for in the dark, You have given in Jesus Christ. Amen.

fields.title: The God in the Cave
fields.body_html:
And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn. LUKE 2:7

The second part of The Everlasting Man opens, like the first, in a cave. Chesterton had begun the human story with the man in the cave, drawing pictures of animals on the walls. He began the story of Christ with the God in the cave — for an old tradition, going back to the early church, holds that the stable at Bethlehem was a cave in the hillside, of the kind in which the shepherds of that country still drove their cattle at night.

Where extremes meet

Chesterton found in the birth at Bethlehem a paradox so great that all the literature and art of Christendom had not exhausted it. The Creator of the universe had become a helpless baby. The hands that made the stars could not yet reach up to touch the faces of the animals around Him. In the chapter of The Everlasting Man called The God in the Cave he put it in a sentence that sums up the whole of it: “the hands that had made the sun and stars were too small to reach the huge heads of the cattle.” And: “Bethlehem is emphatically a place where extremes meet.”

For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace. ISAIAH 9:6

The shepherds and the wise men

He then turned to the two groups of visitors who came to the manger. The shepherds, he said, stand for the common people of every land, who had made the myths and told the stories, and who had always longed for a God who would come near to them. The wise men from the east stand for the philosophers and the learned, who had searched the heavens for the meaning of things. Both found what they were looking for in the same place. The myths had dreamed of a god who came down among men; the philosophers had reasoned towards a God of truth; and here, in a cave, the dream and the reason met. Of the shepherds he wrote, in the same chapter: “The shepherds had found their Shepherd.”

And it came to pass, as the angels were gone away from them into heaven, the shepherds said one to another, Let us now go even unto Bethlehem, and see this thing which is come to pass. LUKE 2:15
Now when Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judaea in the days of Herod the king, behold, there came wise men from the east to Jerusalem. MATTHEW 2:1

Danger at the manger

Chesterton insisted that the Christmas story is not merely sweet. There is something defiant in it. A king in Jerusalem heard of the birth and sent soldiers to murder the children of Bethlehem, and the holy family fled by night into Egypt. The child in the cave was born into a world that wanted Him dead, and from the very first the powers of the earth recognised Him as a threat. Christmas, for Chesterton, was a feast of joy, but also of vigilance and of battle: the opening of a war that would end at the cross and the empty tomb.

Then Herod, when he saw that he was mocked of the wise men, was exceeding wroth, and sent forth, and slew all the children that were in Bethlehem, and in all the coasts thereof, from two years old and under. MATTHEW 2:16

Weighing it

This is one of the loveliest chapters Chesterton wrote, and it faithfully celebrates the central wonder of the faith: that the Word was made flesh. Evangelical readers will receive it with joy.

A small note may be added. The cave at Bethlehem is an ancient tradition, and a probable one, but the Gospels speak only of a manger and do not say where it stood. Chesterton built a great deal on the image, and he did so knowingly, as a poet; the reader should enjoy the image without mistaking it for Scripture. More importantly, in this part of the book Chesterton writes, as a Catholic, with a warm devotion to the mother of Christ that goes beyond what the New Testament says of her. Evangelicals honour Mary as the one whom all generations call blessed, and as a model of faith and obedience; they do not pray to her or ascribe to her the place that Roman Catholic devotion gives. The wonder of Bethlehem is the Child.

fields.body_html:
But whom say ye that I am? MARK 8:29

The heart of The Everlasting Man is its account of the life, death and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Chesterton called it, in a phrase that he admitted was much too weak, the strangest story in the world. His aim in these chapters was to strip away the familiarity that keeps us from seeing it, and to look at the Christ of the Gospels with fresh eyes.

Reading the Gospels as new

He began, in the chapter called The Riddles of the Gospel, with an experiment of the imagination. Suppose, he said, that a man who had never heard of Christianity sat down and read the four Gospels for the first time. What would strike him? Not, Chesterton argued, the meek and mild teacher of popular imagination, who said pleasant things about loving one another. He would be struck by something much stranger: a figure who spoke with terrifying authority, who gave startling commands, who rebuked demons in the tone of a man taming a lion, who told stories of breathtaking beauty and uttered sayings that seemed to turn the world upside down. He would find not an endless stream of platitudes but a series of riddles.

And it came to pass, when Jesus had ended these sayings, the people were astonished at his doctrine: for he taught them as one having authority, and not as the scribes. MATTHEW 7:28–29

The catastrophic claim

Above all, the new reader would stumble over the claim. This man, a Jew among Jews, spoke as though He were God. Chesterton thought that the honest reaction to such a claim was not polite admiration but shock. He wrote that it was no fault in a man who heard it for the first time to think it impious or insane; that stumbling over it is the first step towards understanding it. “Stark staring incredulity,” he wrote, “is a far more loyal tribute to that truth than a modernist metaphysic that would make it out merely a matter of degree.” Either the claim was true, or the man who made it was a blasphemer or a madman; what He could not be was a merely good teacher with an unusual vocabulary.

Then the high priest rent his clothes, saying, He hath spoken blasphemy; what further need have we of witnesses? MATTHEW 26:65

Readers of C. S. Lewis will recognise the shape of this argument. Lewis, who read The Everlasting Man as an unbeliever in his twenties, later set out a similar case in his own words, and it became one of the best-known arguments of modern apologetics.

The road to the cross

Chesterton then followed the story to its end. He noticed that Jesus did not wander into His death by accident. He set His face towards Jerusalem, and walked steadily into the trap that He knew was waiting. And in the trial and crucifixion, Chesterton saw every power of the ancient world combine against Him: the priests and the politicians, the philosophers and the mob, the empire of Rome and the religion of Israel. All that was best and worst in humanity joined in one verdict. He wrote of the cry from the cross with a hushed reverence, as a mystery too deep for words, in which, as he put it, “God had been forsaken of God.”

And at the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani? which is, being interpreted, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? MARK 15:34

The first day of a new creation

And then the dawn. The friends of Jesus came to the tomb on the third day and found it empty. Chesterton wrote that they hardly realised the full meaning of what they saw: that the old world had died in the night, and that a new creation had begun. In the last sentence of the chapter called The Strangest Story in the World he wrote that “in a semblance of the gardener God walked again in the garden, in the cool not of the evening but the dawn.” The God who had walked in Eden in the cool of the day, and been hidden from by fallen man, now walked in another garden at sunrise, risen from the dead.

Jesus saith unto her, Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou? She, supposing him to be the gardener, saith unto him, Sir, if thou have borne him hence, tell me where thou hast laid him, and I will take him away. JOHN 20:15
And they heard the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the cool of the day. GENESIS 3:8

Weighing it

These chapters are Chesterton’s greatest achievement, and they are thoroughly faithful to the Gospels. His insistence that Christ cannot be reduced to a teacher of morals, his vivid sense of the strangeness of the Gospel story, and his radiant account of the resurrection have strengthened the faith of countless readers.

One thing should be added, gently. Chesterton writes about the cross with deep reverence but says less than the apostles say about what it accomplished. He sees the drama of the passion — the world rejecting its Maker, the Son crying out in the darkness — and he sees the new creation that follows. The New Testament adds, with great plainness, that Christ died for our sins, bearing in His own body the penalty that we deserved, so that we might be forgiven and justified. Chesterton believed this. But the reader who has been moved by his account of the strangest story should go on to the epistles, where its meaning is explained.

For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures; and that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:3–4

The reader should also know that in the same chapters Chesterton speaks of the New Testament as the selection made by the authority of the church from a larger mass of early Christian writing. Evangelicals believe that the church did not create the canon but recognised it: that the books of the New Testament carry their authority from God, who inspired them, and that the church’s task was to receive what He had given.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read one Gospel through this week as though you had never heard it before. What strikes you as strange?

2. Have you been content to admire Jesus as a good teacher? What would it mean to take His claim with full seriousness?

3. Read Mark 14–15 and notice how every group in the story turns against Christ.

4. Read John 20:1–18 slowly. Imagine the dawn in the garden.

5. Read the chapters of The Everlasting Man called The Riddles of the Gospel and The Strangest Story in the World, in the Ochorus library.

Lord Jesus Christ, You asked Your disciples who they said You were, and the question still stands.
I confess that You are the Christ, the Son of the living God, who spoke with authority and walked steadily to the cross for me.
Thank You for bearing my sins, and for being forsaken so that I might never be.
Thank You for the empty tomb and the dawn in the garden. Make me a part of Your new creation, and let me live today in the light of Your rising. Amen.

fields.title: The Five Deaths of the Faith
fields.body_html:
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. MATTHEW 16:18

The Everlasting Man ends, before its summary, with a short chapter about the history of the church after the apostles. Chesterton did not attempt to tell that history in detail. He wanted to point out one strange pattern in it, which he thought was itself a kind of evidence for the faith. He called the chapter The Five Deaths of the Faith.

Too old to die, and too young

The religions and philosophies of the ancient world, he observed, had a way of simply lasting. They grew old and sleepy, and went on for centuries side by side, never quite believed and never quite abandoned. Christianity had the opposite fate. Again and again in its history it has seemed to die — to be hollowed out from within by doubt and worldliness, until only an empty shell remained and every clever man expected its end. And again and again it has come back to life, not as an old religion lingering on, but as a new one, with young men and women throwing themselves into it as though it had just been discovered. Chesterton put the pattern into a single sentence: “Christianity has died many times and risen again; for it had a god who knew the way out of the grave.”

I am he that liveth, and was dead; and, behold, I am alive for evermore, Amen; and have the keys of hell and of death. REVELATION 1:18

Five times

He named five occasions on which the faith had seemed finished. The first was the age of Arius in the fourth century, when the church, newly made respectable by the emperors, seemed ready to settle into a reasonable religion with a Christ who was less than God; and then the faith of Nicaea, defended by Athanasius and others, rose up and threw the reasonable religion down. The second was the age of the Albigensians in the Middle Ages, when a gloomy philosophy that despised the body and the material world spread through southern Europe. The third was the scepticism of the Renaissance humanists; the fourth, the mockery of Voltaire and the Enlightenment; the fifth, the confident materialism that followed Darwin in the nineteenth century, which was still in the air when Chesterton wrote. In each case, he said, the faith appeared to be going to the dogs. And in a phrase that has become proverbial: “In each of these five cases it was the dog that died.”

Thou fool, that which thou sowest is not quickened, except it die. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:36

Why it rises

Chesterton did not think this pattern was an accident. A religion that was merely a human invention, he argued, would grow old and die like every other human thing. Christianity keeps rising because it is not, at bottom, an idea at all. It is a Person, who has Himself been dead and is alive for evermore. The church is His body, and what happened to Him happens again and again to it: it is betrayed, crucified, buried, and raised.

There is great comfort in this for believers in a season when the faith seems to be dying around them. Chesterton wrote in an age when the clever people were certain that Christianity was finished. A century later it is the faith of far more people, in far more nations, than it was when he wrote, and many of the confident philosophies that were to replace it are themselves forgotten.

The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever. ISAIAH 40:8

Weighing it

Chesterton’s chapter is a bracing antidote to despair about the church, and its central claim is thoroughly biblical: the gates of hell shall not prevail against the church that Christ builds, because Christ Himself has conquered death.

Evangelical readers will want to add something to his list, and will notice where he draws its lines. For Chesterton, by the time he wrote this book, the faith that kept rising was the faith of the Roman Catholic Church, and the revivals he had chiefly in mind were Catholic revivals. Protestant readers will see other resurrections in the same history that he passes over: the recovery of the gospel of grace at the Reformation, the evangelical awakenings of the eighteenth century under Wesley and Whitefield, the great missionary movement that carried the faith to every continent. They will also observe that the deaths of the faith have often come from within, when a church has kept its forms and lost its gospel. The pattern Chesterton noticed holds; but what rises each time is not an institution as such. It is the Word of God and the Spirit of life, raising up faithful people out of a dead church.

Wilt thou not revive us again: that thy people may rejoice in thee? PSALM 85:6
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Are you discouraged about the state of the church in your country or your town? Read Revelation 1:9–18 and take heart from the risen Christ.

2. Learn the story of one of the revivals of church history — Nicaea, the Reformation, the Evangelical Awakening — and thank God for it.

3. Consider where your own faith has grown cold and formal. Ask God to raise it again.

4. Pray for a revival of true faith in a place you know that seems spiritually dead.

5. Read the chapter of The Everlasting Man called The Five Deaths of the Faith, in the Ochorus library, and The Key Teachings of Athanasius of Alexandria for the story of the first.

Lord Jesus Christ, You were dead, and You are alive for evermore, and You hold the keys of death and hell.
Thank You that Your church has died many times in the eyes of the world, and that You have raised it again every time.
Where my faith has grown cold, and where Your church around me has kept its forms and lost its life, revive us again.
Keep me from despair, and make me a part of the next rising, for the glory of Your name. Amen.

fields.title: The Holy Joy of St Francis
fields.body_html:
I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me. GALATIANS 2:20

In 1923, a year after he became a Catholic, Chesterton published a short life of St Francis of Assisi. It is not in the Ochorus library, and nothing of it is quoted here, but it belongs in any account of his teaching, because in Francis he found the saint who most perfectly embodied the things he loved: wonder, gratitude, humility, poverty, chivalry and, above all, joy. He had loved Francis since boyhood. The book is less a biography than a portrait, and it tells us almost as much about Chesterton as about the little poor man of Assisi.

The troubadour of God

Francis was born in the Italian town of Assisi around 1181, the son of a rich cloth merchant. As a young man he was gay, generous, extravagant and full of dreams of knighthood. Then, by a series of crises — a captivity, an illness, a vision, an encounter with a leper whom he forced himself to embrace — he was turned around. He renounced his inheritance, stripping off his fine clothes before the bishop and his father, and gave himself to a life of poverty, prayer and preaching. Others joined him, and the order of friars that grew from his little band spread across Europe.

Chesterton saw Francis as a troubadour, a wandering singer of romance, who had transferred all the chivalry and courtesy of the troubadours from a human lady to God. The most memorable image of the book is of Francis standing, as it were, on his head. Chesterton insisted that Francis’s poverty was not gloomy. There is much in Francis, and in Chesterton’s portrait of him, that every Christian may admire: his love of Christ, his humility, his joy, his care for the poor and the outcast, his delight in creation. fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God! how unsearchable are his judgments, and his ways past finding out! ROMANS 11:33

We have covered a good deal of ground in fifteen short chapters, and it might seem that Chesterton was a man of many subjects. He was. He wrote about fairy tales and madmen, about paradox and tradition, about the cave painters and the shepherds of Bethlehem, about St Francis and the common man, and he wrote about all of them in essays, novels, detective stories, poems, plays, biographies and books of argument. But beneath the variety lay a single astonishment, which he first felt as a young man on the edge of despair and never lost. It was that the world is a gift; that a gift implies a Giver; and that the Giver has come into His world, in Jesus Christ, to rescue it.

One thread

Look back over the chapters and the thread appears. The wonder he learned in the nursery was wonder at a world that need not have been. The madman’s closed circle and the thought that stops thought were what happens to a mind that will not receive the world as a gift. Cosmic patriotism was the loyalty of a creature to the home his Father made. The furious opposites and the romance of orthodoxy were the shape of the truth about the God-Man, held without compromise. Joy was the secret at the root of it all. Tradition was the faith handed down by those who had received it before us; humility was the posture of a creature before his Maker; the dignity of ordinary things was the glory of a world in which God Himself had worked at a carpenter’s bench. The man in the cave was the creature made in God’s image; the God in the cave was that Creator made flesh. The strangest story in the world was His life, death and rising. The five deaths of the faith were the echoes of His resurrection in His church, and St Francis was one man who saw it all and was glad.

For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen. ROMANS 11:36

What to do with it

Chesterton is one of the most enjoyable writers who ever lived, and that is both his gift and his danger. It is possible to read him for the pleasure of his paradoxes and his jokes and to come away merely entertained. He would have thought that a failure. He did not write Orthodoxy to be admired; he wrote it because he believed it was true, and because he wanted his readers to believe it too.

But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. JAMES 1:22

So here is the plainest counsel this book can give. Go back to the chapter that challenged you most, and act on its points for reflection, one at a time, over the coming weeks. Then open Orthodoxy and The Everlasting Man in the Ochorus library and read Chesterton for yourself, slowly, enjoying him. And then go past him, to the Scriptures from which every true thing he wrote was drawn, and to the Lord whom he loved.

Two things to carry

Carry away, first, the habit of gratitude. Chesterton held on to his sanity, and found his way to Christ, by a thread of thanks. You can do the same. Every morning brings a new sun, every meal is a gift, every person you meet is an image of God. Say grace over all of it, as he did, and you will find that thanksgiving opens the eyes.

Carry away, second, the joy of the faith. Christianity is not a burden to be carried or a theory to be defended with a grim face. It is the best news a human being can hear: that God made the world, that God loves it, that God has entered it, and that God has risen from its grave. If you believe that, you may be sad about many things, but you cannot be sad at the root.

Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:16–18

A last word about the man

We have tried to be honest in these pages. Chesterton came to believe in the authority of the Roman Church, in the invocation of Mary and the saints and in the Catholic sacraments, and evangelical readers will differ from him there. He held economic and political opinions, distributism among them, that are opinions and not doctrines. He wrote, in some places, about the Jewish people with a prejudice that was wrong and that his own principles condemn; and though he stood early and firmly against the Nazi persecution, the pages remain, and a fair companion must say so.

None of this has been raised to diminish him. It has been raised because it is true, and because the Christian faith he defended is a religion of truth-telling and of repentance. Generations of believers of every tradition have found in Orthodoxy and The Everlasting Man a joyful, fearless and faithful defence of the faith they share, and they have been right to do so. They have also been right to read him with their Bibles open.

But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:7

Chesterton died on the fourteenth of June, 1936, at his home in Beaconsfield. Near the end he said that the issue was now clear, between light and darkness, and that everyone must choose his side. He had chosen his long before. He had spent his life telling a sceptical world that the light is real, that it has come into the world, and that the darkness has not overcome it. The right response to him is not admiration but thanks — to God for the gift of the man, and to God for the gift of the light.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Return to the chapter of this book that most challenged you. Read it again, and act on the first of its points this week.

2. Begin reading Orthodoxy in the Ochorus library this month, a chapter at a sitting.

3. Start the habit of grace before ordinary things: before work, before a walk, before opening a book.

4. Ask God to show you any prejudice in your own heart against any group of people, and repent of it.

5. Read 1 Thessalonians 5:16–24 aloud, and end in thanksgiving.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You made the world out of nothing, and You have come into it in Jesus Christ to make it new.
Thank You for the servant whose life and words we have been considering, and for the many who have found their way to You through him.
Do not let me stop at enjoying him. Bring me to the Christ he served, and make me a doer of Your word.
Give me eyes full of wonder, a heart full of thanks and a tongue full of charity, until the gigantic secret is a secret no longer, and I see You face to face. Amen.

fields.title: His Books, and Where to Start
fields.body_html:
Of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh. Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man. ECCLESIASTES 12:12–13

Chesterton wrote some eighty books, and it is not always easy to know where to begin. Two of the best are in the Ochorus library. Many others are in the public domain and freely available elsewhere; a few of his later works remain in copyright in some countries and are available from their publishers. What follows is a short guide, arranged for usefulness rather than chronology, with a suggested order of reading, and a note on the friend he most influenced.

Begin here

Orthodoxy (1908). The natural starting point, and in the Ochorus library. His account of how he came to believe, from the fairy tales of the nursery to the creed. It is the book behind chapters three to eleven of this companion. Read it a chapter at a sitting, and do not worry if some of the jokes are about people you have never heard of; the argument carries through.

The Everlasting Man (1925). His greatest book, also in the Ochorus library. The whole human story, from the cave painters to Christ, told to show that man is no mere animal and Christ no mere man. It is the book behind chapters thirteen to sixteen. Read it after Orthodoxy; it is longer and denser, and the second part, on Christ, is the summit.

His other Christian books

Heretics (1905). The book that provoked Orthodoxy: essays on the leading thinkers of his day, from Kipling to Shaw, each found wanting. It is in the public domain. Read it after Orthodoxy to see the argument from the other side.

St Francis of Assisi (1923). A short, glowing portrait of the saint he loved best, written soon after his reception into the Catholic Church. See chapter seventeen of this book.

St Thomas Aquinas (1933). A short, lively introduction to the great medieval theologian, admired by scholars of Aquinas. It remains in copyright in some countries.

The Thing (1929) and The Well and the Shallows (1935). Later collections of essays, mostly defending the Catholic faith; they include the famous parable of the fence described in chapter ten. The second remains in copyright in some countries. Evangelical readers will find much to enjoy and much to weigh.

His stories

The Father Brown stories (from 1911). Five collections of detective stories about the small, shabby priest who solves crimes because he understands the human heart. The Innocence of Father Brown (1911) and The Wisdom of Father Brown (1914) are the best places to begin, and are in the public domain.

The Man Who Was Thursday (1908). A wild, funny and finally awe-inspiring novel about a poet who infiltrates a council of anarchists, each named after a day of the week. Written in the same year as Orthodoxy, and best read alongside it.

The Napoleon of Notting Hill (1904). A comic fantasy about a London borough that goes to war for its independence, and a celebration of local loyalty.

His poems

The Ballad of the White Horse (1911). A long ballad about King Alfred and his victory over the Danes, full of the Christian hope that holds on when everything seems lost. Lepanto (1911), a stirring shorter poem about the great sea battle of 1571, is also much loved. Both are in the public domain.

His life and opinions

What’s Wrong with the World (1910). His case for the family and the home against the reformers of his day; see chapter twelve. The Outline of Sanity (1926) sets out his distributism.

Charles Dickens (1906). One of the finest books on Dickens ever written, and a good introduction to his love of the common man.

Autobiography (1936). His own account of his life, finished shortly before his death. It remains in copyright in some countries.

For his life, Maisie Ward’s Gilbert Keith Chesterton (1943) was written by a friend who knew the family; Ian Ker’s G. K. Chesterton: A Biography (2011) is the fullest modern account. Readers who want to understand the charges of antisemitism discussed in the introduction will find them examined in detail in Simon Mayers’s Chesterton’s Jews (2013). The Ochorus author page carries a shorter biography.

A suggested order

For a first year with Chesterton: Orthodoxy; a volume of Father Brown; The Everlasting Man; The Man Who Was Thursday; St Francis of Assisi; Heretics; and then, as the appetite grows, The Ballad of the White Horse and his essays. Read Orthodoxy twice. Nearly everyone who loves it has.

Chesterton and C. S. Lewis

No account of Chesterton’s influence would be complete without the friend he never met. C. S. Lewis first read a volume of Chesterton’s essays in 1918, as a young soldier in a military hospital in France, and liked him at once, while still a convinced atheist. A few years later, in his twenties and still an unbeliever, he read The Everlasting Man, and he later described it as the first book that let him see the Christian account of history as one coherent whole. He counted it among the books that brought him to faith. The shape of some of Lewis’s best-known arguments — the claim of Christ that leaves no room for a merely good teacher, the longing that points beyond the world, the conviction that old books guard us against the errors of our own age — can be traced in Chesterton before him, though Lewis made each of them his own. Lewis’s books remain in copyright, and are not quoted here; the Ochorus library holds The Key Teachings of C. S. Lewis and Portraits of Courage – C. S. Lewis, which tell his story and describe his teaching.

Chesterton himself was influenced by George MacDonald, whose fairy story The Princess and the Goblin, read in childhood, he said had changed the way he saw everything. MacDonald’s Unspoken Sermons are in the Ochorus library. Readers should know that MacDonald hoped for the final salvation of all, and rejected the teaching that Christ bore the penalty of sin in our place; evangelical readers will want to weigh both.

Three counsels for reading him

Read him with the Bible open. Chesterton was a journalist, not an apostle, and he would have been the first to say so. Where he is plainly scriptural, receive it with joy. Where he goes beyond Scripture, weigh it.

Read him slowly. His paradoxes come so fast that they are easily skimmed. Stop at the ones that strike you, and turn them over until you see what they mean.

And read him as he would have wanted: not as an end in himself, but as a signpost. Close the book, look at the world with new eyes, and give thanks to the One who made it and came into it to save it.

Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me. JOHN 14:6

One of the finest books on Dickens ever written, and a good introduction to his love of the common man. Autobiography (1936). His own account of his life, finished shortly before his death. It remains in copyright in some countries. For his life, Maisie Ward’s Gilbert Keith Chesterton (1943) was written by a friend who knew the family; Ian Ker’s G. K. Chesterton: A Biography (2011) is the fullest modern account. Readers who want to understand the charges of antisemitism discussed in the introduction will find them examined in detail in Simon Mayers’s Chesterton’s Jews (2013). The Ochorus author page carries a shorter biography. A suggested order For a first year with Chesterton: Orthodoxy; a volume of Father Brown; The Everlasting Man; The Man Who Was Thursday; St Francis of Assisi; Heretics; and then, as the appetite grows, The Ballad of the White Horse and his essays. Read Orthodoxy twice. Nearly everyone who loves it has. Chesterton and C. S. Lewis No account of Chesterton’s influence would be complete without the friend he never met. C. S. Lewis first read a volume of Chesterton’s essays in 1918, as a young soldier in a military hospital in France, and liked him at once, while still a convinced atheist. A few years later, in his twenties and still an unbeliever, he read The Everlasting Man, and he later described it as the first book that let him see the Christian account of history as one coherent whole. He counted it among the books that brought him to faith. The shape of some of Lewis’s best-known arguments — the claim of Christ that leaves no room for a merely good teacher, the longing that points beyond the world, the conviction that old books guard us against the errors of our own age — can be traced in Chesterton before him, though Lewis made each of them his own. Lewis’s books remain in copyright, and are not quoted here; the Ochorus library holds The Key Teachings of C. S. Lewis and Portraits of Courage – C. S. Lewis, which tell his story and describe his teaching. Chesterton himself was influenced by George MacDonald, whose fairy story The Princess and the Goblin, read in childhood, he said had changed the way he saw everything. MacDonald’s Unspoken Sermons are in the Ochorus library. Readers should know that MacDonald hoped for the final salvation of all, and rejected the teaching that Christ bore the penalty of sin in our place; evangelical readers will want to weigh both. Three counsels for reading him Read him with the Bible open. Chesterton was a journalist, not an apostle, and he would have been the first to say so. Where he is plainly scriptural, receive it with joy. Where he goes beyond Scripture, weigh it. Read him slowly. His paradoxes come so fast that they are easily skimmed. Stop at the ones that strike you, and turn them over until you see what they mean. And read him as he would have wanted: not as an end in himself, but as a signpost. Close the book, look at the world with new eyes, and give thanks to the One who made it and came into it to save it.
